title: A Classroom With No Clock
passage:
When the wall clock in Class 2-B stopped working, the teacher planned to replace the battery after school. Before she could do it, one student suggested leaving the clock broken for a day. The class laughed, but the teacher agreed as long as lessons were not interrupted. Students still had watches, tablets, and the school bell, so nobody would truly lose track of time.

The next morning, the blank clock face became surprisingly noticeable. Several students looked up at it automatically during the first lesson and then remembered that it was useless. Others checked the time on a tablet instead. During group work, one student kept asking how many minutes were left because she could no longer glance at the wall.

At lunch, the class discussed what they had noticed. Some students said the clock helped them plan. If ten minutes remained, they knew whether to begin a new task. Others said they looked at it too often, especially during difficult lessons. One boy admitted that seeing only five minutes pass sometimes made a class feel slower. Without the clock, he had focused more on finishing the work in front of him.

The teacher used a small timer for activities that needed exact limits, but she did not announce every minute. By the end of the day, students had different opinions. A few wanted the wall clock removed permanently, while most preferred to have it back. The class decided the useful question was not whether clocks were good or bad. It was how often they needed time information and when checking it became a distraction.

The next morning, the clock had a new battery. Students could once again see the time with a glance. Yet for several days, some of them noticed themselves before looking up. That brief pause was the most lasting result of the experiment. The broken clock had made a common object visible by taking away its normal function. It reminded the class that tools can guide behavior so quietly that people may not notice the guidance until the tool disappears.
translation:
2年B組の壁時計が止まったとき、先生は放課後に電池を替えるつもりでした。ところが生徒の一人が、一日だけ壊れたままにしてみようと提案しました。授業を妨げないことを条件に先生も同意しました。腕時計やタブレット、校内ベルがあるので、本当に時間が分からなくなるわけではありません。

翌朝、動かない時計は意外なほど気になりました。何人もの生徒が第一時限中に無意識に見上げ、そのたびに使えないことを思い出しました。グループ活動では、壁を一目見れば済まないため、残り時間を何度も尋ねる生徒もいました。

昼休みに感想を話すと、時計は計画に役立つという意見がありました。残り十分なら次の作業を始めるか判断できます。一方、難しい授業では時計を見すぎるという生徒もいました。五分しか進んでいないのを見ると、授業が長く感じることがあるというのです。時計がない方が目の前の作業へ集中できたとも話しました。

正確な時間制限が必要な活動では先生が小さなタイマーを使いました。最終的に、壁時計をなくしたい生徒も少数いましたが、多くは戻してほしいと考えました。大切なのは時計が良いか悪いかではなく、いつ時間情報が必要で、いつ確認が気を散らすのかという問いでした。

翌朝、時計には新しい電池が入りました。それでも数日間、何人かは見上げる直前に自分の行動へ気づくようになりました。これが実験の一番長く残った変化でした。普段当たり前の道具は、その働きを失ったとき初めて、どれほど静かに行動を導いていたか見えてくることがあります。
